newsitem.title: USA: U.S. undecided on how to run EEP if restarted.
newsitem.headline: U.S. undecided on how to run EEP if restarted.

text.p: The U.S. has not yet decided how to run the Export Enhancement Program if it restarts the subsidy procedures for wheat, U.S. Agriculture Department general sales manager, Chris Goldthwait said in a recent interview.
Top department officials have recently said USDA may dust off the export subsidy program if the U.S. harvests a big wheat crop this summer and the European Union continues to subsidize its exports.

Just before the U.S. put EEP to bed in the summer of 1995 because of tight global grain stocks and high prices, it floated three proposals to reform the program -- a pre-announced bonus system, a quarterly auction and the existing program with some changes.
The issue has languished since the program was shelved and industry officials predicted it would not be resolved in time to make a significant change this year if EEP were restarted.
Goldthwait said the interagency team charged with making the decision has determined to use a modified EEP for sales of flour, vegetable oil and other processed goods.

And he said, "we have basically all the pieces in place so we could go forward very quickly" should the decision be made to go with the third option, a modification of the existing program, for wheat and other bulk commodities.
But Goldthwait added, "Saying that does not prejudge the ultimate decision...if it looked like restart was imminent we would sit with the other agencies and come to a decision on the mechanism."
The other agencies involved in the decision-making process include the State Department, the Treasury Department and the U.S. Trade Representative's Office.

Goldthwait said under a modified EEP, USDA would move from virtually no communication with exporters to supplying information on prices and bonuses most recently approved and what the department believes has changed in the market since those transactions.
"We hope that by speaking specifically, it would give a clearer indication of what we would approve," he said.
U.S. grain groups and exporters had favored a pre-announced bonus system saying it would give exporters more flexibility.
